Philologus
fi-LOL-uh-guhs
proper noun
A believer at Rome greeted by Paul (Romans 16:15); Greek Philologos, “lover of the word” or “fond of learning.”

Biblical Definition

Philologus was a believer in the church at Rome, named among the long list of saints Paul greets at the close of his epistle to the Romans: Salute Philologus, and Julia, Nereus, and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints which are with them. Nothing more is known of him—no deed recorded, no office named, no further word—and herein lies his quiet importance. Philologus is one of the obscure saints of Scripture, known to us by name only because the Spirit moved Paul to greet him; yet he was known fully to God, his name written, the dictionary trusts, in the Lamb’s book of life. The Scripture honors such hidden saints: a book of remembrance was written before the LORD for them that feared Him and thought upon His name; the Lord bade His disciples rejoice that their names are written in heaven; Paul speaks of his fellowlabourers whose names are in the book of life. The dictionary reads Philologus as a representative of the countless unsung believers—the faithful obscure, who hold no office and leave no monument, yet are loved by Christ, greeted by name, and remembered before God. His one-word mention is a comfort to every hidden saint: that no believer is anonymous to God, that the humblest member of the church is named and known and dear to the Lord, and that the book of remembrance holds the names the world forgets.

Webster 1828 Definition

A believer at Rome greeted by Paul (Romans 16:15), of whom nothing more is known; a representative of the obscure, faithful saints, unknown to the world but named and loved by God.

Key Scripture

Rom 16:15 — "Salute Philologus, and Julia, Nereus, and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints which are with them."

Mal 3:16 — "Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name."

Php 4:3 — "And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel, with Clement also, and with other my fellowlabourers, whose names are in the book of life."

Luk 10:20 — "Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the age prizes only the famous and forgets the obscure; Scripture honors the hidden saint, named and loved by God though the world knows him not.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift to name is the age’s idolatry of fame, which measures worth by visibility and forgets entirely the obscure—and which has crept into the church, where celebrity pastors and platformed influencers are honored while the faithful unknown are overlooked. But the Scripture reverses the world’s scale. It pauses to name a Philologus of whom nothing else is recorded, for he was dear to Christ and to the church; and it teaches that a book of remembrance is written before the LORD for them that fear Him, and that the names to rejoice over are those written in heaven—not the names trending on the earth.

The principle to recover is the honor God gives the hidden saint. Philologus held no office we know, did no deed Scripture records, left no monument; yet he is named, because he was known and loved by God. The Lord bids His people rejoice not in visible success but that their names are written in heaven; Paul remembers fellowlabourers whose names are in the book of life. This is a deep comfort to every obscure believer who serves unseen, suffers unnoticed, and will leave no earthly memorial: no saint is anonymous to God. The humblest member of Christ’s body is named, known, and dear to Him, and the book of remembrance holds the names the world forgets.
